quote_check_note: All 16 first-reader quotes were matched against ROOT/pdf/P-1225.txt and ROOT/pdf/P-1231.txt on the page stated, after collapsing whitespace. q10 and q14 match only with the soft hyphen and line break inside 'speci-ficity' and 'iden-tifying' removed; the source typos in q16 ('CE-d', 'classifies') are the extract's own.
strongest_case_against_the_verdict: Three routes, the second and third on quantities the ledger record did not name. (a) Same analyte, same metric type, overlapping symptomatic populations, independent studies: P-1225's plasma p-tau181 AUC of 0.910 lies above P-1231's entire P-tau181 range (0.610-0.840), and P-1225's sensitivity of 86.36% (95% CI 77.29-95.34) excludes P-1231's sensitivity range (67-71%). If picking out A+T+ patients inside a symptomatic clinic sample is at least as hard as separating AD and aMCI patients from controls, an AUC above the literature's range contradicts it. (b) A claim-level conflict: P-1231 finds blood P-tau181 rising with clinical stage (AD vs aMCI ratio of means 1.36, 1.20-1.54, p < 0.001), while P-1225 concludes that plasma p-tau181 was 'not influenced by the stage or the severity of cognitive decline' and detected no difference between MCI and AD dementia. (c) A ratio-of-means route: P-1225's MCI vs SCD ratio (2.91/2.15 = 1.35; delta-method 95% CI about 1.09-1.68, my computation) against P-1231's aMCI-vs-controls P-tau181 ratio, which the abstract's range (1.36-2.16) suggests could be as high as 2.16.
why_it_does_or_does_not_succeed: None of the three survives the source documents. (a) The two AUCs have different target conditions and comparators. P-1225 separates A+T+ patients from other patients within SCD and MCI, with AD dementia excluded, no healthy controls, and T defined by CSF p-tau181 (the index analyte, measured in another fluid). P-1231's range is for AD and aMCI patients against controls. P-1231's figure is a range of study-level results from a 32-study systematic review, not a pooled estimate with an interval, so one further study outside it contradicts nothing. P-1225's own AUC has an approximate 95% interval of 0.82-1.00 from its counts (Hanley-McNeil; the first reader's computation, which I reproduced), which reaches below the top of the range. Neither paper establishes that the biomarker-defined problem is the harder one, and P-1225's authors attribute their higher AUC to the A/T(N) target; its sensitivity is taken at a Youden cut-off chosen in the same sample for that different target. (b) On the one quantity both papers actually measure, the unadjusted ratio of plasma p-tau181 concentration in AD dementia to MCI, they agree. P-1225's means (4.03 vs 2.91 pg/mL) give 1.38 (delta-method 1.08-1.77, my computation) against P-1231's pooled 1.36 (1.20-1.54). P-1225's 'no differences ... between MCI and AD demented patients' is a Bonferroni post-hoc non-significance with 14 and 32 patients, so the difference is one of significance only. Its 'not influenced by the stage' is a different estimand, the stage effect adjusted for AP status, and even there its own coefficient is positive with a 95% CI excluding zero (Diagnosis B = 0.415, 0.051-0.778, p = 0.026). The paper calls that coefficient non-significant only against its 0.0125 threshold. The AD dementia vs SCD ratio (1.87, 1.49-2.36, my computation) also falls inside P-1231's AD vs controls 2.06 (1.39-3.06), although SCD is not a control group. (c) P-1231's text prints no aMCI-vs-controls ratio for P-tau181; it appears only in Fig. 4, which is not in the extract, and the abstract's upper value 2.16 matches no printed P-tau181 comparison. P-1225 has no healthy controls: its SCD patients (30.76% AP+ in Table 2) are not 'cognitively healthy volunteers', and it does not restrict its MCI group to amnestic MCI. The population behind the label differs, which is incommensurability. Gates: task (T1 vs T6), dataset family and validation tier fail with no waiver on record. A C-227-style waiver of the task and design gates for a synthesis set against a primary study would be conceivable only if the quantity were shared. An argument for false_positive exists: the record is itself a filed incommensurability note, and the only shared quantity agrees. It does not displace documented_incommensurability, because the contested AUCs are different quantities. The C-238 precedent, where the contested quantities differed and the one shared quantity agreed, was accepted at G4 as documented incommensurability, as was C-239, a record of the same kind. The first reader's grounds stand; (b) adds a ground they did not name, and it points the same way.
grounds: The two AUCs have different target conditions and comparators: A+T+ against other patients inside SCD and MCI with no healthy controls (P-1225), against AD and aMCI patients versus controls (P-1231).
P-1225's reference standard defines T status by CSF p-tau181, the index analyte measured in another fluid, and its authors attribute their higher AUC to the A/T(N) target rather than to the marker.
P-1231's P-tau181 AUC figure is a range of study-level results from a 32-study systematic review, with no pooled estimate or interval that a single study could contradict.

On the one quantity both papers measure, the plasma p-tau181 concentration ratio of AD dementia to MCI, the results agree (P-1225 4.03/2.91 = 1.38; P-1231 pooled 1.36, 1.20-1.54), and P-1225's non-significant post-hoc difference is a difference of significance only.

P-1225's claim that p-tau181 is not influenced by stage is a pathology-adjusted estimand on which its own stage coefficient is positive with a CI excluding zero (B = 0.415, 0.051-0.778), so it does not oppose P-1231's stage gradient.
No ratio-of-means comparison of MCI against controls is available: P-1231 prints no aMCI-vs-controls P-tau181 ratio in its text, and P-1225 has no healthy control group.
The task, dataset-family and validation-tier gates fail with no waiver on record.

The ratios of means, their delta-method intervals and the Hanley-McNeil interval are my computations from the printed means, SDs and counts; neither paper reports them.
corrections_to_first_reader: quantity_b and ground 1 call P-1231's cases 'CLINICALLY diagnosed'. P-1231 says only that AD and aMCI participants 'conformed to AD and MCI diagnostic criteria' (p.2) and does not say whether biomarkers entered those diagnoses. What holds is that P-1231 names no biomarker-defined target condition, and that is enough for the verdict.

quantity_b says the 32-study range spans 'mixed assays'. Section 3.7 does not name the assays behind its AUC ranges; the ELISA, IMR and SIMOA comparison in Section 3.2 concerns the ratio-of-means analyses, so 'mixed assays' is an inference.
source_notes: P-1225's accuracy figures are not mutually consistent: PPV 79.17% (19/24) and NPV 90.32% (28/31) imply 22 AP+ and 33 AP- patients, which would give specificity 84.8% and accuracy 85.5%, not the printed 82.5% and 84.21%; the text gives 36 AP- patients. The ROC denominator is therefore uncertain, but the approximate AUC interval barely moves (standard error about 0.045 on either count) and the verdict is unaffected.
P-1225's abstract gives the AP-status coefficient as B = 1.670 (1.097-2.244), while the text and Table 4 give 1.627 (1.006-2.248).

P-1231's aMCI-vs-controls P-tau181 ratio appears only in Fig. 4, which is not in the extract; the abstract's P-tau181 range of 1.36-2.16 has an upper value that matches no printed P-tau181 comparison (AD vs controls is 2.06), so it cannot be attributed from the text.
